name: Totalitarianism
summary: Totalitarianism is a form of rule that seeks total control of society: a single mass party led by one person, an all-embracing ideology, terror by a secret police, monopolies over communication and arms, and central direction of the economy. Arendt adds that it destroys private life as well as public life and treats people as superfluous. It is defined by its structure, so it takes no position on most economic, religious or social questions.
scope: Totalitarianism as a generic type of rule, answered only from the scholarship that defines it: Arendt's The Origins of Totalitarianism (and the Stanford Encyclopedia's account of it) and the six-trait model of Friedrich and Brzezinski as a reference dictionary reports it. The doctrines and texts of Nazi Germany, Stalinism, Italian Fascism and other member regimes are not evidence here; each has its own entry, and the family's positions do not answer for them nor theirs for it.

sources.title: Hannah Arendt
sources.author: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.usedFor: Scholarly summary of Arendt's account of totalitarianism: total terror, camps, superfluousness, world domination.

one-party-rule.rationale: Friedrich and Brzezinski's syndrome, as Marshall summarises it, joins an elaborate total ideology to a single mass party led by one person, and Arendt describes movements built on the Leader's will as the party's law.

total-state.rationale: Marshall glosses the term as 'the total state', comprehensive and all-embracing, and Arendt's 'total domination' reaches private life as well as public life.

party-controls-media.rationale: A monopoly of the means of communication is one of the six defining elements in Friedrich and Brzezinski's model; Arendt adds that propaganda aims at organisation rather than persuasion.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Arendt dates the first stage of totalitarian rule to the liquidation of open and secret resistance in any organized form, after which terror is the regime's normal content.

leader-cult.rationale: Marshall notes a tendency to a personality cult around the single leader, and Arendt calls the Leader irreplaceable because the whole movement exists to transmit his will.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Arendt says totalitarian rule defies all positive laws, even those it made itself such as the 1936 Soviet Constitution, and that the Leader's will is the party's law.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Arendt contrasts positive laws, which stabilise human action, with totalitarian rule that defies them and has no legally rooted hierarchy of authority, which is the opposite of governing by known standing laws.

person-over-state.rationale: Arendt holds that the real mission of the apparatus is to make human beings superfluous, reducing each to an interchangeable bundle of reactions, which treats persons merely as means.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Under the central idea of the 'objective enemy', categories of people lose all legal standing regardless of conduct, so equal rights before the law cannot hold.

harm-principle.rationale: Arendt stresses that totalitarian domination, unlike older tyrannies, destroys private life as well and does not limit coercion to protecting others from harm.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Arendt says totalitarian rule kills inner spontaneity and that its education aims to destroy the capacity to form convictions, the reverse of encouraging individuality.

self-ownership.rationale: The regime's aim, in Arendt's account, is to turn people into interchangeable bundles of reactions, which denies any person's rights over their own body and labour.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Terror is held to be the essence of the form, applied to people who have done nothing, so initiating force is central rather than wrong.

political-violence-never.rationale: Arendt identifies total terror as the essence of totalitarian government, justified by the supposed laws of nature or history.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Totalitarian rule suspends legal protections against internal enemies as a permanent condition rather than in an emergency, so it agrees that a government may do so.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Arendt describes ideological thinking as deducing everything from one premise with a consistency found nowhere in reality, and says totalitarian rulers act regardless of utility or self-interest.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: A monopoly on arms is another of the six defining elements Marshall lists.

limit-guns.rationale: A regime monopoly on arms, as Marshall lists it, rules out private armament, though gun ownership as a policy question is not discussed.

empower-police-military.rationale: Arendt makes the secret police the sole organ of power, which supports more police authority, while noting that totalitarian regimes neglect the army, so the record points both ways.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Arendt reports the unconditional loyalty of members and a hierarchy trained to transmit the Leader's will to all ranks.

public-service-media.rationale: With a monopoly over the means of communication, media independent of government control cannot exist.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Arendt notes that the seat of power is a mystery by design and that the less known an institution is, the more power it holds, the opposite of open access.

democracy-best.rationale: Arendt describes totalitarian movements as holding parliamentary government in contempt, and their rule rests on a single party rather than competitive choice.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Arendt shows totalitarian rule defying even the constitutions it keeps on paper, so a written rights guarantee cannot limit it.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Central direction and control of the economy through bureaucratic coordination is one of the six defining elements.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Arendt says totalitarianism in power uses the state for its long-range goal of world conquest, and the SEP repeats that it aims at world domination.

national-mission.rationale: The aim of global rule gives the regime a mission to extend its order to other peoples, though Arendt stresses that it disregards nationality.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Marshall's dictionary entry describes the 'total state', and Arendt's account has the individual wholly subordinated to the movement and state, placing the individual's obligations above individual rights.

notes: Searched all themes in Arendt's Part Three, the Stanford Encyclopedia entry and the dictionary definitions: government and law, liberty, means, world, economy (only the central-direction trait), society and culture. Friedrich and Brzezinski's book and Linz's chapter were not openly available, so the six-trait model is cited through Marshall. Religion, church and state, family and gender, class, minority and secession questions were searched in Arendt and the dictionary entries and the record states nothing on them. Economic, religious, family, ecological and technology statements are null because the family is defined by structure rather than by programme.
